section_summary: This section covers diplomatic despatches, State Department memoranda, telegrams, and related press clippings from late May to late August 1937 documenting Japanese domestic politics and foreign relations. Major subjects include Foreign Minister Naotake Sato's foreign policy pronouncements and growing firmness toward China, the collapse of General Senjuro Hayashi's cabinet following the April 1937 elections, and the formation of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's coalition cabinet. The documents also analyze the creation of the Planning Board under Koki Hirota, early diplomatic and military ramifications of the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in North China, and the secret court-martial sentencing of General Jinzaburo Mazaki for his role in the February 26 Incident.

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum reviewing Ambassador Grew's despatch on Japanese Foreign Minister Naotake Sato's recent speeches on foreign policy.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (JWB / Wm)
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 2443 analyzing public addresses delivered by Japanese Foreign Minister Naotake Sato. It notes that Sato remained confident in discussion and reason for resolving international issues, while highlighting a noticeable stiffening in Japan's stance toward China due to army pressure. The memo also calls attention to Sato's view that Japanese-American relations were generally satisfactory and trade friction was being alleviated.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 2443 on Foreign Minister Sato's Speeches

subfiles.about: Despatch and four enclosures analyzing recent public speeches and diplomatic conversations by Japanese Foreign Minister Naotake Sato regarding foreign policy and Sino-Japanese tensions.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reviews Foreign Minister Naotake Sato's speeches of May 17 and May 24, 1937, as well as diplomatic conversations held on May 26. Grew concludes that while Sato advocated economic cooperation, peaceful diplomacy, and free trade, his stance toward China reflected increasing firmness influenced by Japanese military pressure, especially following recent incidents in Swatow and the customs patrol. The despatch includes newspaper clippings of Sato's addresses to prefectural governors and the Tokyo Free Trade Association, as well as memoranda of conversation between American diplomats (Grew and Eugene H. Dooman) and Foreign Minister Sato and Vice Minister Kensuke Horinouchi.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2443: Recent Speeches by Foreign Minister Sato (with Enclosures)

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum analyzing the formation, composition, and political implications of the newly installed Konoe Cabinet in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum details the formation of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's cabinet on June 4, 1937, following the formal acceptance of the Finance portfolio by Okinobu Kaya. It examines key cabinet appointments, including Koki Hirota as Foreign Minister, Eiichi Baba as Home Minister, Gen Sugiyama as War Minister, and Mitsumasa Yonai as Navy Minister, noting the balance between military, bureaucratic, and political party interests. It also analyzes initial Japanese press and public reactions, as well as Foreign Minister Hirota's statements regarding Japanese-American and Sino-Japanese relations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Composition of the New Japanese Cabinet

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum reviewing Tokyo Despatch No. 2454 on the resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet and its significance for Japanese politics.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews Ambassador Grew's despatch concerning the 119-day tenure and resignation of General Senjuro Hayashi's cabinet. It notes that the resignation was intended as a concession to political parties to head off deeper opposition following Hayashi's sudden dissolution of the Diet and subsequent election defeat. It concludes that while not a sweeping victory for party government, the episode demonstrated that the military could achieve national objectives more effectively under a leader with greater political acumen.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 2454 on the Fall of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Despatch with newspaper clippings examining the resignation of Prime Minister Senjuro Hayashi and his cabinet following political confrontation with the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes the collapse of the short-lived cabinet of General Senjuro Hayashi, which resigned on May 31, 1937, after holding office for only 119 days. The report details Hayashi's error in dissolving the House of Representatives on March 31 as an act of discipline, the subsequent April 30 general election that reaffirmed party opposition, and Prince Konoe's intervention criticizing Hayashi's exclusion of party members. Enclosures include articles from The Japan Advertiser documenting the chronology of the Hayashi regime and Prince Konoe's remarks on the political impasse.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2454: Fall of the Hayashi Cabinet (with Enclosures)

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum examining the appointment of Foreign Minister Koki Hirota to head the newly established Planning Board.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum analyzes Tokyo Despatch No. 2466 concerning Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's selection as head of the Planning Board (Kikakucho). It points out that the board was designed as a coordinator of government policy and national budgeting, serving as a compromise between military desires for state-controlled planning (favoring Eiichi Baba) and financial interests (favoring Kaya or Yoshino). It notes that Hirota's appointment represented a limited concession to the military while leaving the board's ultimate influence uncertain.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 2466 on Appointment of Hirota as Head of Planning Board

subfiles.about: Despatch with the text of Imperial Ordinance No. 192 and an editorial analyzing the establishment of the Planning Board and the appointment of Koki Hirota as its head.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on Premier Konoe's appointment of Foreign Minister Koki Hirota to lead the Planning Board (Kikakucho), created by Imperial Ordinance No. 192 on May 13, 1937. Grew explains that the board was created in response to military pressure for organs to coordinate state socialistic reforms and national policies, but appointing Hirota represented a compromise between army factions favoring Eiichi Baba and business circles favoring Okinobu Kaya or Shinji Yoshino. Enclosures provide an English translation of Imperial Ordinance No. 192 from the official gazette Kampo and a Japan Advertiser editorial on the history of cabinet super-commissions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2466: Hirota Appointed Head of Planning Board (with Enclosures)

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum analyzing the political stability, strengths, and weaknesses of the newly formed Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum assesses Tokyo Despatch No. 2469 regarding the viability of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's administration installed on June 4, 1937. It highlights the expected cooperation of the Minseito and Seiyukai parties, the prior consent of the Army and Navy to retain Ministers Sugiyama and Yonai, and concerns over Home Minister Eiichi Baba's ties to military state socialism. It also mentions concerns regarding Konoe's frail health and speculation that Koki Hirota might be groomed as a potential successor.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 2469 on the Viability of the Konoye Cabinet
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs / Sumner Welles

subfiles.about: Despatch and memorandum of conversation reporting on the installation, ministerial personnel, policies, and foreign relations outlook of the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed report on the installation of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's cabinet on June 4, 1937, listing all ministers and analyzing the political dynamics behind its formation. Grew notes that Konoe's appointment of party politicians without requiring them to renounce party affiliation eased parliamentary tensions, though business circles remained wary of Home Minister Eiichi Baba. The despatch encloses a memorandum of conversation from June 7, 1937, wherein newly appointed Foreign Minister Koki Hirota affirmed that the 1934 Hull-Hirota goodwill messages would guide U.S.-Japan relations and indicated an intention to seek concrete rather than abstract solutions in relations with China.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2469: Konoe Cabinet Installed June 4, 1937 (with Enclosure)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Telegram No. 217 regarding the Sino-Japanese conflict in Wanpinghsien and potential cabinet changes.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 217 of July 21, 1937 (decimal file 793.94/8889), regarding developments in the Sino-Japanese conflict in the Wanpinghsien area. It notes reports concerning the possible succession of Prince Konoe by General Sugiyama as Premier if the North China crisis deepened, discounting Hirota as a potential successor.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 217 Regarding North China Conflict and Premiership Succession

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram conveying intelligence from a reliable foreign informant on Japanese troop mobilization, the North China conflict, and possible premiership succession.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports information from a reliable foreign informant indicating that Prince Konoe's illness is genuine and that General Sugiyama would succeed him as Premier if the North China crisis worsened. The informant and the U.S. Military Attaché assess that Japanese mobilization has been only partial, estimating troop deployments to North China from Japan, Chosen, and the Kwantung Army, and characterizing the situation as negotiations progressing with armed intervention. The report also conveys the belief that Soviet Russia will not intervene militarily due to internal purges, and that China does not intend to wage serious war against Japan.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 217: North China Situation and Potential Succession to Konoe

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck discussing Japan's decision-making in the Sino-Japanese crisis.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: This document file note records a memorandum dated August 10, 1937, by Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs (filed under 793.94/9487, referenced in 894.00/752). It summarizes the question of whether Japan will fight in China, stating that financial considerations alone will play little role and that the ultimate decision will be made by the armed forces rather than diplomats, bankers, or business leaders.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Memorandum by Hornbeck on the Sino-Japanese Situation

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 2519 concerning the court-martial and sentencing of General Jinzaburo Mazaki.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews Ambassador Grew's report that General Mazaki was sentenced by court-martial to six years' imprisonment for complicity in the February 26, 1936 military rebellion. It highlights the Embassy's conclusion that the sentence primarily demonstrated the high military command's determination to maintain discipline within the army. It also notes that while differences of opinion may exist regarding foreign policy, there was no evidence of internal struggle hindering the execution of policy in North China.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 2519 on the Trial of General Mazaki

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting the confidential court-martial and six-year prison sentence of General Jinzaburo Mazaki for his involvement in the February 26, 1936 revolt.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports information obtained from a former Japanese diplomat indicating that General Jinzaburo Mazaki was recently sentenced by court-martial to six years' imprisonment for having prior knowledge of and encouraging the February 26, 1936 military rebellion. Grew observes that while commentators might seek broader political significance, the sentence was fundamentally an assertion of army discipline by the high military command. He notes that while court advisers like Tsuneo Matsudaira attempted to urge restraint regarding North China, there was no active internal struggle preventing the implementation of continental policy once the incident began.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2519: Arrest and Trial of General Mazaki
